The robotics club at Harmon Ridge. I started it, I'm the coach, I've been doing it since fall 2018, so my second year here. My first year, 2017-18, I was just surviving, I wasn't starting any clubs. Then a couple of my eighth graders saw a VEX IQ video on YouTube and kept asking, and I said okay, if you find me eight kids we'll try it.

So the first year it was eight kids and one kit that we borrowed from the high school. One kit! They took turns. We met Tuesdays and Thursdays after school in my room, and honestly I knew nothing about robots. I learned with them, I watched the videos at night. The kids figured out the building faster than me. What I could do was the structure, like the engineering notebook, the design process, making them test and write down why something failed instead of just ripping it apart.

It grew pretty fast. By last year, 2025, we had three teams and 28 kids, and a waiting list. We have girls on every team which I'm really proud of, the first year it was seven boys and one girl, now it's close to half.

The money. In 2022 I wrote a grant to the Desert Sky Community Foundation, it's a local foundation, and we got $12,000. That paid for four new kits, the field, the competition fees, and the bus to tournaments. Before that I was paying for stuff myself a lot, which, don't tell my husband. The PTA helps a little too, we do a bake sale.

Competitions. We go to the regional qualifiers, usually three or four a season, they're on Saturdays in Henderson and North Las Vegas mostly. And in 2024 we won state, well, okay, let me say it properly. One of our teams qualified for the Nevada state championship in 2024, that was the first time for our school, and at the regional qualifier before that they won the Judges Award, which is for the engineering notebook and how the team explains their process. At state they finished 11th out of about 40 teams. For a Title I school with kits that are mostly secondhand, that felt like winning. The kids cried, I cried.

The part that connects to what I want to do next: I ended up building a whole little curriculum for the club. The new kids every fall used to just get thrown in, and the older kids would get frustrated. So I made a six-week onboarding sequence, building basics, then coding blocks, then the notebook, with little challenges at the end of each week, and the returning kids lead the stations. I put it in Canvas too, of course. Now the new kids are competition-ready by October instead of January. I'm the one who designed that, it's mine.

Also I think it changed how I teach my regular classes, more design challenges, more letting kids fail and fix.

I don't want to oversell my own tech skills here though. I can do the block coding and help with basic VEX Python, like reading what a kid wrote and spotting the loop that's wrong, but I'm not a programmer. The kids who go on to the high school robotics team know way more code than me by ninth grade.

What else. Parents. I do all the parent communication, permission slips, the group chat. It's a lot of logistics, honestly maybe more logistics than robotics.

So yeah, that's the club. It's probably the thing I'll miss most if I leave teaching.
